Aegean regions and western and central Anatolia (II) – Overall favourable development
In these important regions for winter crop
production, sowings took place in December, just
after the first rain following a prolonged summer
drought. Germination was ensured by mild
temperatures up to 2 °C above the LTA and by welldistributed rainfall in December, which was still
below the LTA (– 10 % to – 50 %) but restored soil
moisture in the upper layers. January was marked by
two short cold spells, but no significant damage
occurred. February presented contrasting conditions:
above-average temperatures (up to + 6 °C in Konya
and Kırıkkale) and abundant precipitation supported
crop development, while a pronounced radiation
deficit (up to – 30 % in Orta Anadolu), associated
with the continued rainfall, limited biomass
accumulation.
As a result, crop development was moderate,
reaching average growth stages by early March
across the main producing regions. Only in the
Aegean regions (e.g. in Manisa), where the radiation

deficit was less pronounced and temperatures were
higher, did crops develop more rapidly and
accumulate above-average biomass.
A dry spell in the first 15 days of March favoured
radiation accumulation and offered good growing
conditions despite below-average temperatures.
From mid March, temperatures increased and,
together with returning rainfall, enabled a normal to
slightly advanced development of winter crops in
both the Aegean regions and western Anatolia (e.g.
in Ankara). Slightly less favourable conditions were
observed in central Anatolia (e.g. in Kayseri), where a
more pronounced temperature accumulation deficit,
particularly in early March and since 10 April, slightly
delayed crop development. Nevertheless, the wellreplenished soil moisture and water reservoirs
support positive expectations for the remainder of
the season, including the upcoming sowing of
summer crops.

4. Country analysis
4.1 European Union
France – Repeated heatwaves lowered yield outlook
The country experienced an extremely hot and dry
review period, marked by two heatwaves following
the hot spell already experienced at the end of May.
The most severe episode occurred at the end of June
and was particularly persistent in the western
regions, while another heatwave affected the
country in the first half of July. Both events were
accompanied by a pronounced rainfall deficit.
Impacts on winter crops remain limited, although
accelerated grain filling may have slightly reduced
yield potential in the north, with spring barley most
affected. The greatest concern is for rainfed summer
crops. In western and southern France, the late-June
heatwave coincided with the early flowering of

maize, while the July event hampered full flowering,
resulting in a substantial reduction in yield potential.
With dry conditions forecast to persist until the end
of July, the possibility of further downward revisions
cannot be excluded. Rainfed sunflowers were
similarly affected, whereas soybean benefited from
a higher share of irrigated fields. Irrigated crops
have so far remained in fair condition, although
irrigation restrictions could limit yield potential if the
hot and dry weather persists. In northern France,
heat stress has also reduced the yield potential of
sugar beet and potatoes. Our yield forecasts have
been revised downwards, particularly for summer
crops, to below the five-year average.

Hungary – Drought conditions compromise yields
Above-average daily temperatures predominated
during the review period, and a record-breaking
heatwave hit Hungary in the second half of June.

drought since 1991. Inadequate water supply and

crops have been suffering from critically low soil

expectations remain favourable, as the heat stress

Grain maize - Sowing in full swing in southern Europe, set to accelerate elsewhere
The grain maize sowing campaign is progressing
rapidly in parts of southern and western Europe,
while it is slightly delayed in the Balkan peninsula,
and has just started elsewhere. In Greece, sowing

drier-than-usual conditions in March and April,
offsetting the overly wet February and allowing a

reached the threshold required for maize
establishment, and sowing is about to start within
the optimal time window. The campaign is also
expected to begin shortly in Belgium. In Germany
and Poland, sowing has commenced following a
cold and dry early spring, which preserved good

seedbed conditions. However, topsoil is locally very

Hungary and Bulgaria, sowing has not yet started
on a large scale, as the cold spell at the beginning of
April delayed field operations and higher
temperatures and rain are needed to support
sprouting and emergence. In Romania, sowing has
just started.

5. Extended analysis for Türkiye
Türkiye – Excellent winter crop season

The 2026 growing season in Türkiye has been wet
and cool, supporting an exceptionally favourable
yield outlook for all winter crops. Summer crops
have benefited less, but are in nonetheless
favourable condition. This special section on Türkiye
continues the analysis published in the April edition
of the JRC MARS Bulletin and focuses on crop
conditions from 1 May to 18 July.

Since early May, agroclimatic conditions have been
largely uniform across the country. The start of May
was wetter (e.g. in Konya, with precipitation at
> 150 % compared with the LTA) and cooler (e.g. in
Sivas, with temperatures at least 2 °C below the
LTA) than usual, with rainfall totals often above
150 mm. As a consequence, winter crop growth,
already behind schedule, was further delayed, and
flowering occurred 10 to 30 days later than usual,
depending on the region. This delay, which would
typically be expected to expose winter crops to heat
stress in June, was actually beneficial this year. In
June, precipitation diminished and crops entered
grain formation and grain filling under optimal
conditions, well supported by high radiation. The
yield formation period was mild and soil moisture
progressively decreased; crops had more time than
usual for grain filling, resulting in record-high yield
expectations in most regions. Maturity was reached
from late June to early July and the harvest has
started. Only in the Central Anatolia Region are
winter crops still in the ripening stage and yet to
reach maturity.

Germany – Favourable conditions despite lack of rainfall
The review period was characterised by average
temperatures beneficial for the steady phenological
development of winter crops. Wheat and barley
advanced rapidly through stem elongation, while
rapeseed entered flowering stage slightly earlier
than usual, especially in the west. Low rainfall in
April has been increasingly constraining soil water
availability, especially in lighter sandy soils. While
the low rainfall levels were beneficial for sowing and
field operations, initial signs of water stress became
noticeable in winter crops and, after emergence, in

summer crops as well. Rainfall returned across the
country in early May, but water availability remains
scarce in the south. Overall, crops remain in good
physiological condition, and the rainfall forecast in
May should help to improve soil water availability
and preserve yield potential.
Our yield forecasts for winter and spring barley were

the yield outlook for summer crops remains in line
with the trend.

Poland – Adverse weather conditions reduced the yield outlook for winter crops

Poland during the reporting period, further lowering
soil moisture levels, particularly in the east of the
country (e.g. Mazowiecky, Lubelskie), and negatively
affecting winter crop growth. Near-average rainfall
is currently forecast, which would bring some relief
and help to avoid additional deterioration.
Near-seasonal temperatures prevailed until late
April, when a cold spell with freezing temperatures
occurred from 27 to 30 April, coinciding with the
flowering stage of rapeseed and the beginning of

the reproductive stages of winter cereals. This event
is expected to have caused flower abortion, thereby
reducing the yield potential of rapeseed. Remote
sensing images indicate below-average biomass
accumulation in several regions (e.g. Opolskie,
Wielkopolskie), reflecting the generally deteriorated
crop conditions. We have therefore revised our yield
forecasts for winter crops downwards.
The sowing campaign for spring and summer crops
is coming to an end. Our yield outlook for these
crops follows historical trends.

with large parts of the country experiencing the wettest

now entering the flowering stage under unfavourably
dry conditions across most of western Ukraine, raising

Continued spring rain supports exceptional crop growth
Across the Maghreb region, the pattern of above-average rainfall starting in late December 2025 has

3. Winter hardening and frost kill
De-hardening of winter crops has continued in southern, western and central Europe, with a partial or high
level of frost tolerance in northern areas. Frost around 10 April may have caused local crop damages in
central Europe, primarily in more sensitive winter barley and rapeseed crop stands.

Hardening is the biophysiological process whereby
winter cereals gain low-temperature tolerance to
withstand the freezing conditions that occur during
the winter dormancy period.
Winter wheat was almost or fully hardened in all of
northern and eastern Europe and most of western
Europe until the beginning of March. Above-average
temperatures in March and early April supported a
rapid de-hardening process in southern and western
Europe, though a cold air intrusion in the second
week of April halted its progress. As of 18 April,
winter cereals had de-hardened in southern and
western Europe and in most of central Europe and
the Black Sea area. There, mild conditions reduced
the frost tolerance of winter crops by up to two
weeks compared with the average. Our model
simulations still present an advanced or fully

hardened stage in the northern parts of Ireland, in
Germany and Poland and in the Baltic and
Scandinavian countries. However, frost tolerance is
steadly decreasing with increasing temperatures in
spring.
Due to the low temperatures in April, minor frost
damage to winter barley and winter rapeseed
cultures can be expected in central Poland, Czechia
and Slovakia, eastern Hungary and northern
Romania.
Weather forecasts until the end of April suggest
continued below-average temperatures across most
of Europe, which would slow down the progress of
de-hardening in the north. However, the lack of frost
conditions in de-hardened areas suggests that
further frost damage is unlikely to occur.

Denmark and Sweden – Good conditions at the start of the season
Above average temperatures were reported during the
analysis period, resulting in cumulative temperatures
close to 30 % above the LTA in both countries, and up
to 60 % in Östra Mellansverige. Conversely,

frost kill in southern Sweden. Spring sowing started on

Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland – Cautiously positive start of the season

higher than usual was reported across the four
countries, with cumulative temperatures ranging
between 50 % and 100 % above the LTA. Conversely, a

precipitation more than halved in most regions.

throughout the reporting period allowed the winter
crop harvest to progress swiftly. The winter barley

wheat and rapeseed harvests are still progressing.

soil moisture may locally reduce yields, especially in
Jutland. Similarly, tuber crops in Denmark could be

affected by locally dry conditions and will require
monitoring. Green maize is performing well overall,
especially where irrigation is possible. Our yield
forecasts have been revised slightly upwards for
soft wheat and spring barley in Sweden, and remain
above the five-year average for other winter crops.

been revised slightly downwards to account for the
continued dry conditions, but remain above the fiveyear average.

Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland – Fair prospects despite excessive rainfall

values, precipitation was above average throughout
July across the region, most notably in Latvia and
Lithuania, where cumulative rainfall was 30 %

spread of diseases, especially in potatoes. Timely

crops remain in fair to good condition overall, as
confirmed by satellite signals in line with the LTA.
Winter crop harvests are well advanced, and the

spring barley harvest has just begun in Latvia and
Lithuania, though wet soils are locally complicating
fieldwork. Although no impact of excessive moisture
is expected on yields, quality could be affected.
Summer crops, if adequately protected against pests
and diseases, should benefit from the current
conditions. Our yield forecasts have been revised
slightly downwards for tuber crops to reflect wet
conditions, and kept close to the five-year average
for other crops.

Germany – Favourable crop development despite variable weather
During the first half of May, a cooler period
temporarily slowed phenological development –
particularly that of winter cereals entering the stem
elongation and heading stages – but also helped
maintain soil moisture through reduced evaporation.
In the second half of May, rapidly increasing

Summer crop emergence and early establishment
benefited from warm temperatures but were locally

hampered by insufficient topsoil moisture. The first
half of June brought rainfall that reduced water
stress and mitigated potential damage. Winter crops
are now at the grain-filling stage and summer crops
are flowering; the positive crop development
trajectory, especially in the south and east, will be
challenged again by high temperatures and limited
rainfall forecast for the remainder of June.

and summer crops, with yields up to 5 % above the
five-year average.

Poland – Winter crops remain affected by water stress
Although rainfall was near or above average across
most of Poland during the reporting period, with
temperatures close to seasonal levels, precipitation
was insufficient to reverse the soil moisture deficits
that had developed earlier in the season.
As a result, winter crops kept growing under water
stress during the critical flowering and early grainor pod-filling stages. Both crop model simulations
and satellite imagery point to below-average
biomass accumulation in several regions, reflecting
the persistent impact of limited water availability.

Consequently, the yield outlook for winter crops has
been further reduced, albeit slightly, remaining in
line with or somewhat below the five-year average.
Harvesting is expected to begin locally in the coming
days.
Spring and summer crops continued their vegetative
development under generally favourable thermal
conditions, but further rainfall will be required to
sustain growth. Their yield outlook remains
unchanged, in line with the five-year average.

Benelux countries – Slow crop growth during cold and heat in May
A cold spell in mid May temporarily slowed crop
development, particularly for winter cereals. This
was followed by a pronounced heatwave with scarce
rainfall at the end of the month, increasing crop
water demand. For winter cereals, these conditions
probably accelerated reproductive development and
potentially shortened the grain-filling period. Spring
crop development benefited from the warm
conditions, but growth rates temporarily slowed
down when the increasing water demand was not
fully met by the depleted topsoil moisture.

Precipitation in early June alleviated these
constraints and supported fair development across
all crops. Overall, crop conditions remain favourable;
however, the fAPAR signal shows that the
exceptionally positive winter crop biomass anomaly
observed earlier in the season has diminished, with
biomass levels now around the seasonal average.
Our yield forecasts for spring crops have been
maintained, while those for winter cereals have been
reduced by 1–2 % compared with last month,
although they are still above the five-year average.

Slovenia and Croatia – May rainfall temporarily relieved crops
Storms in mid May brought much-needed precipitation
across most of Slovenia and Croatia, accompanied by
cold temperatures, winds and local hail. Damage to
summer crops and barley has been reported in BrodPosavina (south-eastern Croatia). Elsewhere, soil
moisture was replenished to almost average levels, but
this could not fully compensate for the impacts of the
rainfall deficit in early spring. Since the second half of
May, temperatures have increased, sometimes
exceeding 30 °C, with limited precipitation up to mid

June, mainly in Slovenia. Winter cereals are at the
grain-filling or ripening stage, with the early-sown ones
close to harvest; the corresponding fAPAR signal is
close to average in both countries. While additional
precipitation is needed to sustain summer crop growth,
weather forecasts point to precipitation only in northern
Slovenia in the next 10 days. Our yield forecasts
remain mostly unchanged, below the five-year average
for soft wheat in Slovenia and winter crops in Croatia,
and above average for summer crops.

2. Agrometeorological overview
2.1 Meteorological review (1 March – 18 April)
Spring weather was spatially variable: much of continental Europe was drier than usual, while parts of the
Mediterranean experienced above-average precipitation from Atlantic storms; temperatures were above
average in the north and west, while contrasting hot and cold spells occurred in North Africa and some
Mediterranean areas.

The weather synthesis map summarises the most
distinct anomalies during the reporting period
compared with the 1991–2025 long-term average
(LTA) for the same period. Precipitation deficit and
surplus are absolute and relative deviations from
the LTA. Temperature surplus and deficit indicate a
substantial deviation in accumulated temperature
from the LTA. Cold spells indicate where
temperatures were below – 2 °C and below the
10th percentile for a period of five consecutive
days, while hot spells indicate where temperatures
reached 30 °C and the 90th percentile for a period
of five consecutive days.

A distinct precipitation deficit characterised most
of central and eastern Europe, while also affecting
parts of the west and north. Total precipitation was
below 30 mm in many areas, representing 50 % or
less of the LTA. In most of Europe, there were 2–5
fewer wet days than average, with larger deficits
locally: up to 10 fewer wet days in north-western
Spain, along the Adriatic coast of the western
Balkans and in northern Romania and south-western
Ukraine.
A temperature surplus occurred mainly in Finland,
most of Sweden and the Baltic countries, northeastern Poland, north-western France and northern
and central Italy. Average daily temperatures in
these regions were up to 6 °C or more above the
LTA. Elsewhere in Europe, except Ireland, southern
Spain and Portugal, the Balkans and western and
central Türkiye, temperatures were mildly above
average (up to 3 °C). Minimum daily temperatures

stayed above - 5 °C, except in mountainous areas,
and there were fewer cold days than usual.
Western and north-eastern coastal Morocco, northwestern coastal Algeria and parts of northern Tunisia
were affected by hot spells, while northern Morocco
and easternmost Türkiye experienced a
temperature deficit, with average daily
temperatures up to 3 °C below the LTA.

Benelux countries – Hot and dry weather increasingly impacts summer crops
Rainfall was almost absent during the reporting
period, while persistent heat further aggravated crop
water stress. Winter cereals largely escaped these
adverse conditions, as the preceding heat had
advanced crop maturity and harvest by several
weeks, ahead of the exceptionally hot and dry July–
August period. Nevertheless, the shortened grainfilling period slightly reduced winter crop yield
expectations, with forecasts below 2025 levels but
remaining around the five-year average.

By contrast, summer crops were strongly affected.
Potato bulking has slowed down, resulting in smaller
tubers and advanced senescence; sugar beet growth
has been also increasingly constrained, although to a
lesser extent. Maize has been the most affected,
showing reduced biomass accumulation, locally poor
cob formation and premature senescence; a marked
conversion from grain to green maize is expected.
With no substantial rainfall forecast, further
deterioration is likely. Summer crop yield forecasts
have been notably reduced, now well below the fiveyear average and 2025 levels.

Slovenia and Croatia – Reduced outlook for summer crops under heat and moisture stress
Except for a few days in July, temperatures
remained well above average throughout the
reporting period. A notable heatwave developed in
August, with maximum temperatures repeatedly
above 35 °C and locally reaching 40 °C. The heat
stress hampered photosynthetic activity and limited
biomass accumulation, constraining grain filling for
maize and soybean and causing leaf damage locally.
Precipitation remained below average, exacerbating
the water stress. Overall, unfavourable conditions for

crop growth occurred in all agricultural regions, and
the heat combined with a persistent rainfall deficit
rapidly depleted soil moisture, even where the soil
had been adequately replenished in early summer.
Winter crops escaped the stress due to early
harvests, with yield forecasts essentially unchanged.
Summer crops, however, were impacted, and our
yield forecasts have been substantially revised
downwards, especially for grain maize and soybean.
Summer crop yields are now forecast below the fiveyear average for both Slovenia and Croatia.

Hungary – Cold and dry weather challenges crop growth
The previously advanced phenological development of
winter cereals slowed down in April but remains ahead
of average. Remote sensing images indicate fair
photosynthetic activity. For rapeseed, low temperatures
and limited crop water availability constrained
pollination, side stem growth and yield formation.
Severe frost around 10 April and at the beginning of
May, with temperatures locally dropping to –7 °C,
caused damage to flowering rapeseed, orchards and
vineyards, primarily in the north-east, but also in

central and eastern regions. The cold spells delayed the
start and progress of spring sowing. Topsoils remained
dry and dusty due to the continued rainfall deficit so
that the sprouting and emergence of spring crops was
delayed and uneven, with weak, underdeveloped and
locally patchy fields.
Our yield forecasts for winter cereals near or mostly
slightly below the five-year average; but have been
reduced for rapeseed, while staying in line with the
trend for summer crops early in the season.

Italy – Dry emergence for summer crops
In northern and central Italy, the weather was
unusually dry (with precipitation levels at – 50 %
compared with the LTA) and warm (up to + 4 °C above
the LTA), with the analysis period ranking as the third
warmest in our records. This reduced soil moisture in
the upper soil layers, which combined with windy
weather meant that irrigation had to start rather early
in the season, where possible, to maintain the yield
potential of winter crops and foster the emergence of
summer crops. Precipitation in early May helped
sustain maize emergence and first-leaf expansion.

Winter crops, now in the early flowering stage, fare
well.
In southern Italy, April was predominantly dry and
warm, with few well-distributed precipitation events.
The previously wet soils dried up, and growing
conditions became favourable, boosting biomass
accumulation to above average. In Puglia and Sicilia,
durum wheat development remains advanced and is
approaching the grain-filling stage.
Our crop yield forecasts remain slightly above average
for winter crops, while still based on the trend for
summer crops.

Czechia, Austria and Slovakia – Hot and dry weather triggers early maturity
Crop development was marked by moisture deficits,
and an exceptional heatwave hit in late June. Winter
cereals completed the grain-filling stage
prematurely and experienced accelerated
maturation, which will probably lead to reduced
kernel weight and grain quality. This accelerated
development brought forward the winter barley
harvest by up to two weeks, followed by the other
winter cereals. Winter wheat is expected to be the
most affected due to its later phenology, which saw
its grain-filling stage occur during the peak of the
heatwave.

Rainfall in July modestly restored soil moisture
levels but arrived too late to markedly improve
winter crop conditions. Summer crops reached their
most vulnerable growth phases, but water scarcity
still limited flowering and biomass accumulation in
eastern Austria, southern Czechia and western
Slovakia. The weather forecast for the coming days
should ease heat stress, but soil moisture deficits
are likely to continue.
Yield forecasts across crops have been revised
downwards to as low as 10% below the 5-year
average, especially in Slovakia.

Bulgaria – High yield expectations for winter crops

adequate during the late grain-filling stage. The
short heatwave of late June had no effect on grain
formation thanks to advanced phenological
development, due to which the harvest campaign
started early this year and is now progressing well.
Crop model simulations and remote sensing
information indicate well-above-average biomass
accumulation for winter crops; our yield forecasts
have been revised upwards to near-record levels.

moisture to below average in the rooting zone of
summer crops. Despite some rain in July so far, the
limited water supply has started to impact the
cardinal flowering and early grain-filling stages.

accumulation are still near average, satellite images
confirm deteriorating conditions for summer crops.
The yield forecasts for summer crops have been
reduced but remain above average.

Ukraine – Good summer crop outlook despite water deficit risk
Weather was cooler and drier than average across
most of Ukraine during the reporting period. The
relatively dry conditions remained favourable for
winter crop maturation and harvesting. For summer
crops in the western oblasts (e.g. Volyns’ka), soil
moisture remained limited after the already dry
spring, affecting crop conditions. Maize reached
grain filling under favourable conditions in the north,
south and east; soybean, predominantly cultivated in
the west, was more exposed to the dry soils.

The harvesting of winter crops was completed in
July; yield forecasts are unchanged for wheat and
rapeseed, while the barley forecast has been revised
slightly upwards, reflecting favourable conditions
during the final grain-filling stage of spring barley.
The grain maize yield forecast has also increased,
supported by favourable crop conditions, particularly
in the centre and north. The soybean yield forecast
remains close to the average, with less favourable
conditions in the west partly offset by favourable
conditions in central regions.

Türkiye – Delayed but fair summer crop conditions
The winter cereal harvest ended in most regions in
early July, with very satisfactory results. Only in
Kayersi did crops remain in the field up to the end of
July, but the delay did not cause harm and the
season concluded with optimal yield expectations.
Summer crops are still delayed in development due
to late sowing. Most notably, the second crop cycle in
Şanlıurfa has been significantly delayed and crops
have not yet emerged; the remote sensing signal

points to a reduction in sown area for the summer
cycle, in line with the increased surface area
dedicated to winter crops this year. In the remaining
regions (e.g. Adana, Hatay, Samsun), biomass
accumulation is favourable, and summer crops are
around flowering with average summer
temperatures and sufficient soil moisture and water
for irrigation. Therefore, our summer crop yield
expectations are 5 % above the five-year average.

Benelux countries – Heat accelerates harvest and raises risks for summer crops
Exceptionally hot conditions since mid June have
accelerated crop development across the Benelux
countries. A shortened grain-filling stage and forced
ripening caused barley and wheat to mature
unusually early, and harvesting advanced rapidly;
local storms increased yield variability.
Rainfall in the first half of June initially replenished
soil moisture, but the subsequent heatwave and
limited rainfall sharply increased the water demand
of spring and summer crops. Potato and maize
performance became increasingly dependent on

irrigation. Potato bulking slowed in some fields, while
maize entered flowering under increasing heat and
moisture stress, which reduced biomass
accumulation and raised concerns for yields. Sugar
beet canopies remained well developed, although
foliar disease pressure requires monitoring. Our yield
forecasts for winter cereals are unchanged, while
those for potatoes and maize have been revised
downwards by 1–3 %. For most crops, yield
expectations remain below 2025 levels but above
the five-year average.

Slovenia and Croatia – Warm conditions accelerated crop growth and harvesting, with variable
yields
Storms in mid June resulted in hail damage in parts
of eastern Slovenia and eastern Croatia. Northern
Croatia received substantial precipitation across the
reporting period, while southernmost Slovenia and
easternmost Croatia continued to experience deficits
in rainfall and soil moisture. Above-average
temperatures since the heatwave in late June have
accelerated winter cereal development, leading to
early maturity and a short and earlier-than-usual
harvest campaign. Overall, yields for winter cereals
and rapeseed are highly variable, depending on the

extent of storm damage, local moisture stress and
access to irrigation. Summer crops have shown good
tolerance to the high temperatures of recent weeks,
and a temporary decrease in temperatures is
forecast. In Slovenia, both winter and summer crop
yield forecasts have been revised slightly
downwards. In Croatia, yield forecasts have been
revised upwards for winter crops to near the fiveyear average, while remaining unchanged for
summer crops, above the last five-year average.

Greece and Cyprus – Above-average yield outlook
In Greece, favourable weather conditions since early
spring have continued to support winter crops.
Adequate rainfall and generally mild temperatures
sustained good biomass accumulation and fair crop
development, with winter cereals currently ranging
from stem elongation to heading and flowering stages.
Impacts related to excess moisture have been reported
only locally. Meanwhile, the sowing of summer crops
has been largely completed under favourable
conditions, and the emerged crops are faring well.
Maize and sunflowers are currently at emergence to

first-leaf stages, while potatoes are in vegetative
development.
In Cyprus, the rainy and overall favourable season has
supported very good development of winter barley,
with biomass levels remaining well above average. A
large share of fields has already been harvested for
wilted silage, while the remaining crops are progressing
through ripening and are expected to be harvested in
late June.
Our yield forecasts in both countries are above the
five-year average.

Ireland – Weather turned favourable, benefiting crops
After a wet start of spring, a dry period at the end of
April allowed the overly wet fields to dry and provided
a favourable window for the delayed field operations
to be carried out. Accordingly, disease pressure from
Septoria and yellow rust observed in some fields could
be kept under control. Sustained by favourable soil
moisture levels, winter cereals are currently in the
heading stage, slightly ahead of the seasonal average.
Rapeseed is also well advanced, with some plants

entering the pod development stage following an early
onset of flowering. Spring barley sowing was
completed, although slightly delayed compared with
the optimal window. After the reduced yield
expectations reported last month, our crop yield
forecasts remain unchanged, slightly below the fiveyear average for cereals and slightly above for
rapeseed.

Hungary – Low yield expectations for all summer crops
Extremely dry and hot weather prevailed in Hungary,
with above-average temperatures since late July
and precipitation in the range of 5–25 mm; only
Nyugat-Dunántúl and some north-eastern areas
received more rainfall, and even that was still below

With a rainfall deficit already in effect since April,
the drought situation worsened in July. Summer
crops suffered from inadequate water supply and
heat stress. Our model simulations indicate
accelerated crop development with shortened grain

filling and reduced biomass accumulation. Maize and
sunflowers are in very poor condition, as confirmed
by remote sensing images. By mid August, numerous
crop stands had already dried in Hungary’s lowlands.
Several grain maize fields have been harvested as
green maize to avoid further losses.
Our yield forecasts have been reduced to 20 %
below the five-year average for sunflowers and
30 % below for maize. The harvesting of winter
cereals progressed well but had disappointing yields,
15–20 % below the five-year average.

Italy – Extreme heat reduced yield expectations
Between 1 July and 15 August, summer crops
experienced extraordinary heat stress, with roughly
two out of three days having maximum
temperatures above 35 °C. Very high temperatures
and fairly dry weather, with precipitation since July
almost 50 % less than the LTA in the north-west,
caused extreme evapotranspiration that strongly
depleted soil moisture and reduced the water
available for irrigation. Summer crops, which had
been developing very well until the end of July, have

started to suffer from both heat and water stress
during flowering and grain filling.
Late-flowering varieties of summer crops in
particular endured severe heat stress, undermining
yield expectations that are further constrained by
the limited availability of irrigation water; overall, a
yield reduction is expected for all summer crops.
Our yield forecasts – except those for sunflowers, at
6 % below the five-year average – have been
reduced to around the values for 2003 and 2022,
about 15 % below the five-year average.

Spain and Portugal – Positive yield outlook for winter crops
Following the excessively wet conditions at the end
of winter, average or below-average rainfall
prevailed across most regions of the Iberian
peninsula (e.g. in Castilla-La Mancha and
Extremadura) during the review period. This allowed

France – Unprecedented drought and heat hit summer crops
France experienced the hottest and second-driest
(after 2022) summer at the national level in the
past 20 years. After hot spells already having hit in
May and June, three more heatwaves affected the
country during the review period, while well-belowaverage rainfall further aggravated moisture
deficits, especially in shallow soils. The impact on
summer crops is exceptionally high, particularly in
the west. Irrigated crops have withstood the drought
stress so far, but increasing water restrictions will
constrain irrigation in the coming weeks.

The phenology of all summer crops has been
accelerated by temperature surplus and heat stress.
Grain maize and soybean are currently at grain
filling, while sunflowers have largely reached
maturity. The area of grain maize is expected to
decline further as crops are redirected to silage,
particularly in western livestock-producing regions.
Sugar beet and potatoes are also suffering from the
adverse conditions. Yield forecasts for all summer
crops have been further reduced to 7–30 % below
the five-year average, with maize reaching a recordlow level of 28 % below the five-year average.

Czechia, Austria and Slovakia – Summer drought threatens summer crops
Winter barley was harvested early with average
results, while heat and water stress during grain
filling has raised the risk of substantial yield losses
of later-maturing wheat. Soil moisture deficits
already present in the spring have been exacerbated
since July, and recurrent heatwaves with
temperatures approaching 40 °C occurred across
eastern Austria, western Czechia and western and
southern Slovakia. Summer crops have been most
affected where extreme heat coincided with
flowering and grain formation. Maize suffered from
impaired pollination, restricted biomass

accumulation, premature senescence and poor cob
formation, particularly in shallow soils or where
irrigation was not available. Sugar beet and potatoes
were constrained during intensive biomass
development; wilting and reduced canopy limited the
growth of storage organs, further lowering the yield
potential. Local rainfall was insufficient to restore
depleted soil moisture reserves.
Consequently, yield expectations for summer crops
have deteriorated substantially, with current
forecasts down to 20 % below the five-year
average.

Bulgaria – Favourable conditions for summer crops
Near-average seasonal temperatures during the
reporting period, combined with the absence of heat
stress, provided adequate thermal conditions for
yield formation. While rainfall totals were near
normal in July, even above the LTA in the north-east,
precipitation decreased in August, and the northwestern region of Severozapaden remained drier
than usual for the entire review period.
The favourable rainfall in July kept soil moisture
close to average conditions, providing a satisfactory
water supply for grain maize and sunflowers, apart

from in the north-west. Satellite information
confirms the generally positive picture, indicating
close-to-average or above-average photosynthetic
activity until the end of July. In August, crop
conditions started to show some deterioration. Our
yield forecasts remain above the five-year average
for summer crops, thanks to the generally
favourable conditions during the cardinal flowering
and early grain-filling stages. The rain in July caused
a moderate delay in the harvesting of winter crops,
for which record-high yields are forecast.

Denmark and Sweden – Crops in good condition despite rainfall deficit
Conditions were drier than usual in both countries, with
total precipitation largely below normal. In Denmark,
the cumulative rainfall was close to 70 % of normal
levels. In Sweden, the deficit is more pronounced,
especially in the south (i.e. Sydsverige), where
cumulative rainfall was 25 % of normal levels. With
temperatures close to the LTA, no issues are expected
for crops so far, as according to our models the

simulated soil moisture remains within a reasonable
range. This is further confirmed by a satellite-based
fAPAR signal close to or slightly above normal. The
spring sowing campaign benefited from dry soils and is
nearly complete in both countries.
Our yield forecasts remain aligned with historical
trends for spring crops, while for winter crops they are
now slightly above the five-year average.

Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland – Winter crops starting to be affected by dry and cold
conditions
Lower-than-average temperatures in Lithuania and
Latvia resulted in a slight deficit in accumulated
temperature. A cold snap in late April with night
temperatures below 0 °C for a few days may have
affected flowering rapeseeds. Total precipitation during
the reporting period was around 50 % of normal levels
in the Baltic countries and only close to 30 % in
Finland. However, the cool weather probably limited the
adverse effects of the precipitation deficit.

Spring sowing is near completion in Lithuania and
Latvia, while still progressing in Estonia and Finland.
The impact of the dry conditions on recently emerged
seedlings has been limited so far and will be further
alleviated by the rain forecast for the coming days.
Our yield forecasts remain aligned with historical
trends for spring crops. For winter crops, our forecasts
have been revised to slightly below the five-year
average, accounting for the effects of dry and cold
conditions.

Czechia, Austria and Slovakia – Beneficial warm start to spring
Above-average temperatures prevailed in March across
the three countries and triggered the de-hardening of
winter crops. Precipitation has been very limited,
regionally as low as 20 % of the LTA. The mix of low
precipitation and above-average temperatures was
beneficial for the sowing and early emergence of
spring crops and for the initial development of winter
crops after dormancy. A colder-than-usual start of April
saw minimum temperatures dropping to as low as

– 5 °C, but crops should have largely been able to
withstand these temperatures. Rainfall will be a key
factor in the coming weeks for winter crop
development ahead of the flowering stage, as well as
for spring crop establishment, but is projected to
remain limited by the end of April in the main
agricultural areas.
We maintain our forecasts for winter crops and spring
crops close to the trend.

Bulgaria – Favourable water supply for winter crops
Soil moisture reserves are well replenished thanks to
the wet winter and abundant rainfall in late March and
early April. The phenological development of winter
crops is delayed by 5–10 days due to below-average
temperature accumulation (by – 10 % to – 30 %);
satellite-based indicators show slightly below-average
biomass production, except in the Severoiztochen
region, which shows above-average values. The
flowering of rapeseed has started. Moist and cold
weather in April could increase pest pressure.

The dominantly dry March weather favoured seedbed
preparation for summer crops. Sowing started in late
March but then progressed slowly due to wet and cold
topsoil conditions in the first dekad of April. Low
temperatures have also delayed the sprouting and
emergence of the seeds sown so far. However, the
progress of sowing should accelerate later in April,
even though some rain is forecast. The yield outlook
for winter and summer crops is still in line with the
trend.

Türkiye – Average crop development

The 2026 season in Türkiye so far has been
characterised by generally favourable conditions
supporting an above-average yield outlook.

December rainfall restored soil moisture and
enabled good crop establishment. Since January,

most regions, although frequent cloud cover has
limited radiation. Since March, temperature

the west and delays in the colder eastern regions,
while excessive rainfall and low radiation have
affected parts of the east and the south-east.
Despite these regional constraints, the overall
agronomic perspectives are fair for the ongoing
season.
Weather up to mid April remained suboptimal for
eastern and southern Anatolia, with low
temperatures in the east and abundant precipitation
in the south.

Germany – Summer crops face substantial losses, especially in the south
The effects of accelerated maturation and persistent
water deficits on winter crops have become
increasingly apparent since harvest. Winter barley
achieved average results, but later-maturing winter
cereals experienced shortened grain filling and
premature senescence, resulting in smaller grains
and locally reduced quality. Losses were most
pronounced in southern Germany, while the north
generally performed better.
Summer crops have now become the principal
concern. Prolonged depletion of soil moisture paired
with recurrent heatwaves has strongly constrained

biomass accumulation and reproductive
development. While comparatively favourable
conditions in the north and east support average
yield expectations, southern Germany is facing
considerable losses in spring and summer crops.
Additionally, diseases in potatoes and sugar beet are
threatening yields.
Winter crop yield forecasts have been further
lowered up to 7 % below the five-year average,
except for winter barley, while the yield outlooks for
spring and summer crops have been sharply cut
within 15 % below the five-year average.

Poland – Persistent moisture deficits and heat stress reduce summer crop prospects
Rainfall was unevenly distributed during the
reporting period, with above-average amounts in the
north-east and below-average amounts in the south.
Most rainfall occurred in July, while precipitation
became scarce from early August onwards. Overall,
rainfall was insufficient to alleviate the persistent
soil moisture deficit, which remained particularly
severe across southern Poland. Temperatures were
generally near seasonal levels, with a cooler period
between 20 and 30 July, followed by heat in early
August, when temperatures reached 36 °C or locally

higher. Remote sensing imagery and model
simulations corroborate the challenging summer
crop conditions observed in the south. Their yield
forecasts have been revised downwards to slightly
below the five-year average due to the combined
effects of persistent soil moisture deficits and heat
stress during reproductive stages. The impact on
winter crops remains limited, as harvesting was
already ongoing or crops were already reaching
maturity by this time; our previous yield forecasts
slightly below the average have been maintained.
